This doesn't make sense. I can present an alternate way of looking at it. Say you have 0 mana at time zero. At that moment, you get a burst of 1.5% of your missing mana. Then for the next 5 seconds, you regenerate mana normally. Viewed this way, the burst regeneration is actually more efficient than the gradual style, because you get 5 seconds worth of regeneration immediately, and before the amount regenerated is lessened by your natural regeneration.

So is the burst regeneration better or worse than the gradual regeneration? It depends on the timing of the regeneration ticks and when you expend your mana. Let's say you have a pool of 500 mana and somehow your full combo costs 300 mana. Every 5 seconds, the gradual method ticks. If you cast your combo right after a tick, then you get your scenario and burst regeneration is worse than gradual regeneration. If you cast your combo right before a tick, then you get my scenario and burst regeneration is better than gradual regeneration. In practice, you wouldn't actually time your spells based on a fairly opaque mastery like this (you could, and you'd get slightly better mana efficiency, but it's probably better just to optimize your spell timing for actually important stuff like hitting the opponent or farming). So you're going to get the good case and the bad case roughly 50% of the time each. Therefore there is no expected difference in efficiency between the gradual style of regeneration and the burst style. (I think the gradual method should still be changed to use the burst style however, just because it's simpler).

In summary: you're wrong. About half the time, the opposite scenario occurs which makes up for what you described. The actual result is that there is no difference in efficiency.

The trick with the tank support is to ensure she doesn't initiate onto you in lane (so position slightly behind your marksman). If she initiates onto your marksman, you can win the all-in pretty easily. As soon as the tank goes in on your marksman, the enemy marksman will usually panic and try to run up to follow up. Chances are he won't be paying attention to you. It's extremely easy at this point to catch the marksman in a full combo, which deals enough damage that the enemy marksman has to back up or risk being killed by you. Your marksman should be fine even without you directly helping because the tank can't solo a marksman, so it's more important that you make sure their marksman doesn't follow up. Once the enemy marksman backs off you can 2v1 the tank and kill her.

tl;dr The tank can't solo a marksman but the mage support can. As long as she doesn't engage onto you specifically, you'll win the 2v2.

If your entire team has a certain amount of health points, then rainbow enhancements on one character gives you that amount multiplied by (1/0.99-1) effective health. Health enhancements give another amount multiplied by 1.075 effective health, where that amount is the health of the character. Therefore, health enhancements are better when the health of the character multiplied by 1.075 is greater than the total health multiplied by (1/0.99-1), or when the ratio of the character's health to the team's health is greater than 0.0094 (i.e., the character must contribute more than 0.94% of the team's health, which is almost always true). This is for the case of only one enhanced character on a team. Resistances become more powerful the more of them you stack, and health enhancements don't apply to additional health bonuses (5940 extra health in total) so we'll consider the fully maximized case as well. A team of all rainbow enhancements has (total health + 5940)/0.95 effective health, whereas a health-enhanced team has total health multiplied by 1.075 + 5940 effective health. Health enhancements are better when total health multiplied by 1.075 + 5940 is greater than (total health + 5940)/0.95, or total health multiplied by 1.075 + 5940 is greater than total health multiplied by 1.052 + 6252.63, i.e., when total health is greater than 13976.47, which again is easily achievable by almost any team.

In conclusion, if you want to increase the raw durability of your team in general, health enhancements will always give you more effective health than rainbow enhancements. Color resistances are more effective if you're stacking them to counter a specific threat, but spreading them out in a rainbow fashion is ineffective except as a counter to certain attacks. It's also worth noting that rainbow enhancements will also make recovery more effective, but in general, color enhancements are preferred over health enhancements, which are preferred over rainbow enhancements for meeting thresholds.

When stamina is implemented correctly (i.e. not too restrictive, and not tacked on), it actually prevents players from getting burnt out and improves the players' enjoyment of the game. You can't just tack stamina onto any generic game and expect it to work; you need to build the game around the stamina system to have it be satisfying to the player.

A popular mobile game is a very good example of a successful stamina system that lets players play a reasonable amount and creates a metagame of planning out stamina use, in addition to being monetization for the game. Stamina regenerates at 1 per 3 minutes, players generally have 200-300 max stamina, and a small fee is a full stamina refill (although this is something that most players rarely purchase). Ranking up will also fully restore stamina, and so there is a lot of planning that goes into maximizing stamina use by ranking up at strategic times. Most challenges cost 25 or 50 stamina to attempt. Some challenges are difficult and take upwards of half an hour to complete, while others are trivial to beat in less than a minute. So the player has flexibility in whether they want the stamina to last by playing hard, rewarding challenges or whether they just want to burn it quickly to get lesser rewards.

In fact, there are occasionally scenarios where you can earn enough experience from a challenge that you can use rank ups to refill stamina and run it infinitely. While that seems nice on paper, it actually feels like a bit of a chore. It's nice when you do run out of stamina and then you can stop playing without feeling like you're wasting resources.
